--

The dashboard did not become difficult because it had too many widgets. It became difficult because nobody could explain who owned its data, state, actions, and failures.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

The dashboard looked like a component problem.
It contained charts, tables, filters, summary cards, modals, permissions, loading states, and several API requests. Every feature had its own file, and most components were reasonably small.
The code still felt impossible to change.
Updating one filter required touching the page component, two hooks, a Context provider, three widgets, and a modal stored in a completely different folder. Refreshing one table could trigger unrelated requests. Permission checks appeared in the page, inside buttons, and again inside custom hooks.
The dashboard was visually crowded, but that was not what made it messy.
The real problem was that no one could explain who owned its behavior.
Who owned the selected date range? Who decided when the dashboard was loading? Who refreshed the data after an action? Who knew whether the user could export a report? Who controlled the modal after a row was selected?
The components were separated.
The responsibilities were not.
That changed how I thought about UI architecture. A screen does not become easier to maintain simply because its JSX is divided into smaller files. It becomes easier when every important decision has an understandable home.
1. Small Components Did Not Create Clear Ownership
The first instinct was to divide the dashboard into smaller pieces:
function Dashboard() {
return (
<>
<DashboardHeader />
<DashboardFilters />
<RevenueSummary />
<SalesChart />
<OrdersTable />
<ExportModal />
</>
);
}The result looked organized.
Each component had a focused name. The main file became easier to scan. The folder structure suggested clear separation.
But the page component still owned almost every changing value:
function Dashboard() {
const [dateRange, setDateRange] = useState(defaultRange);
const [selectedRegion, setSelectedRegion] = useState("all");
const [isExportOpen, setIsExportOpen] = useState(false);
const [selectedOrder, setSelectedOrder] =
useState<Order | null>(null);
const [refreshKey, setRefreshKey] = useState(0);
// Data fetching, transformations, permissions,
// retries, modal behavior, and cross-widget refreshes
}The JSX had moved into smaller files, but the dashboard remained one enormous behavioral owner.
Every feature depended on state introduced elsewhere. Widgets received long prop lists. Actions travelled upward before moving sideways into another component. A small interaction could cause the page component and several unrelated children to render again.
This was the first important lesson:
Component extraction changes where markup lives. Ownership determines where decisions live.
Moving a chart into SalesChart.tsx improves organization. It does not establish whether the chart owns its query, loading state, empty state, or retry behavior.
Those are ownership decisions.
A dashboard can contain many small components and still have no clear architectural boundaries.
2. Shared State Was Really Shared Policy
The date range initially looked like ordinary shared state.
The revenue chart used it. The order table used it. Summary cards depended on it. The export action needed it to generate the correct report.
Putting it in the page component worked until every consumer needed a different combination of filter values and update behavior.
Moving it into Context seemed like an improvement:
function DashboardScope({
children,
}: {
children: React.ReactNode;
}) {
const [filters, setFilters] = useState(defaultFilters);
const contextValue = useMemo(
() => ({ filters, setFilters }),
[filters],
);
return (
<DashboardFilterContext.Provider value={contextValue}>
{children}
</DashboardFilterContext.Provider>
);
}The filters became easier to access.
Their ownership did not automatically become clearer.
Context answers which descendants can read a value. It does not explain who defines its meaning, when it should reset, whether it should survive navigation, or which consumers should update when one field changes.
Context also creates a subscription boundary. When its value changes, consumers of that Context can become eligible to render again. Stabilizing the provider object avoids unrelated identity changes, but it does not stop consumers from updating when filters genuinely changes.
If different consumers depend on different parts of a broad filter object, narrower contexts, selector-based subscriptions, or more focused feature boundaries may be more honest.
The filters were not merely shared values. They represented dashboard policy.
They defined the reporting period used by several widgets. They controlled which requests belonged to the same view. They affected export behavior and whether cached results were still relevant.
That policy belonged to the dashboard feature.
It did not belong inside one widget because several widgets depended on it. It did not need application-wide ownership because it had no meaning outside the dashboard.
Shared usage does not automatically mean global ownership.
The correct owner is usually the smallest boundary that genuinely coordinates all consumers.
Persistence is a separate decision.
When filters must support shareable links, bookmarks, reload restoration, or browser back and forward navigation, the URL may become their persistence boundary. The route stores the values, but the dashboard feature still defines what those values mean.
State should usually disappear when the boundary that gives it meaning disappears, unless persistence across navigation or sessions is an explicit product requirement.
3. Data Fetching Had No Consistent Owner
The dashboard used several data-fetching approaches at once.
One widget fetched its own data:
function RevenueChart() {
const revenue = useRevenueData();
return <Chart data={revenue.data} />;
}Another received data from the page:
<OrdersTable orders={orders} />A third read from Context:
const { summary } = useDashboardContext();A fourth refreshed itself through a shared event.
Each approach could be defended locally. Together, they created a screen with no coherent data-ownership model.
The useful question was not whether widget-owned fetching or centralized fetching was universally better.
The real question was which data had to remain consistent.
Widget-owned data worked when a section was genuinely independent:

• it had its own query;

• it could refresh independently;

• its loading state remained local;

• its failure did not invalidate the rest of the screen.
Feature-level orchestration was more appropriate when several widgets needed to represent one coordinated snapshot.
If the revenue chart, summary cards, and regional totals all came from one report request, splitting them into independent queries could produce inconsistent timestamps, duplicate work, and confusing loading behavior.
Data should live where its consistency requirements live.
This is more useful than declaring that every widget should fetch its own data or that the page should own every request.
The physical cache may still belong to a query library. Several components may consume the cached result. The backend may remain the authoritative owner of the records.
UI ownership describes which feature defines why the data is needed, how it is interpreted, and what should happen when it changes.
That distinction became clearer once I separated three ideas:

• Storage: where the data physically exists.

• Access: which components can read or modify it.

• Ownership: which boundary defines its meaning and lifecycle.
Context can improve access without clarifying ownership. A query library can store remote data without owning its business meaning. A feature can own the interpretation of data that is physically cached elsewhere.
4. Loading and Errors Revealed the Real Boundaries
Loading behavior exposed weaknesses that the component tree had hidden.
The dashboard originally had one Boolean:
const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false);That worked while the page performed one request.
It became misleading when the revenue chart, order table, alerts panel, and export action could all perform work independently.
What did isLoading mean then?
Was the dashboard unavailable? Was one widget refreshing? Was an export running in the background? Was stale data still safe to display?
A single Boolean could not answer those questions.
Loading and error behavior forced us to decide which parts of the interface could succeed or fail independently.
If the revenue request failed, could the orders table remain usable?
If the table refreshed, should the summary cards disappear?
Could the user retry one widget without repeating every dashboard request?
Should stale chart data remain visible while a new filter set loaded?
These were not presentation details. They revealed the actual behavioral boundaries.
If one widget could fail and recover independently, its loading, empty, error, and retry states usually belonged with that widget.
If several widgets depended on one atomic report, a feature-level boundary was more honest.
Loading and error boundaries should match the parts of the interface that can succeed or fail independently.
A global spinner can hide several unrelated operations. Completely local loading states can hide that several views must represent one coordinated snapshot.
Failure ownership should follow actual failure behavior.
5. Permissions Were Scattered Through the UI
Permission logic was one of the clearest signs of unclear ownership.
Conditions appeared throughout the JSX:
{user.role === "admin" && <RevenueCard />}
{permissions.includes("orders.export") && (
<ExportButton />
)}
{account.plan === "enterprise" && (
<AdvancedAnalytics />
)}Each condition looked understandable.
Together, they forced presentation components to reconstruct business policy.
A button knew about permission strings. A chart understood subscription plans. A page header checked user roles. Another hook combined account state with a feature flag.
The same capability could be visible in one place and hidden in another because each component interpreted access differently.
The UI needed meaningful capability decisions rather than raw policy ingredients:
const capabilities = getDashboardCapabilities({
user,
account,
subscription,
featureFlags,
});Components could then render decisions that matched their purpose:
{capabilities.canViewRevenue && <RevenueCard />}
{capabilities.canExportOrders && <ExportButton />}
{capabilities.canUseAdvancedAnalytics && (
<AdvancedAnalytics />
)}This did not make the frontend responsible for security.
The backend still had to enforce authorization for every sensitive operation. Hiding a button does not prevent an unauthorized request.
The frontend’s responsibility was consistent presentation.
A component should not reconstruct business policy merely because it needs to hide a button.
The capability layer should also remain scoped to the feature. One application-wide object containing every possible UI permission can become another global owner that no one fully understands.
The backend owned authorization.
The dashboard feature owned how that authorization was represented in the interface.
6. Modals and Actions Exposed the Missing Owner
Modals often reveal whether a feature has a coherent owner.
An order row opened an edit modal. The dashboard page stored the selected order. The modal performed a mutation through a shared hook. The table needed to refresh afterward. A global toast displayed the result.
One action travelled through several unrelated layers.
The original structure looked like this:
function Dashboard() {
const [selectedOrder, setSelectedOrder] =
useState<Order | null>(null);
return (
<>
<DashboardSummary />
<RevenueChart />
<OrdersTable onEdit={setSelectedOrder} />
<EditOrderModal
order={selectedOrder}
onC
